summary: This is the abstract and introduction of Chapter One in Psychology of Learning and Motivation (Volume 74, 2021) by Alicia Forsberg, Eryn J. Adams and Nelson Cowan. The chapter argues that working memory limits act as a bottleneck for long-term learning, and that working memory and long-term knowledge interact in a positive developmental feedback loop. It proposes adjusting learning materials to learners' working memory abilities and prior knowledge to make learning more efficient.
one_line: A 2021 chapter arguing that working memory limits bottleneck long-term learning in childhood and that learning materials should be adjusted to learners' working memory and prior knowledge.
key_facts: The chapter is Chapter One of Psychology of Learning and Motivation, Volume 74, 2021, pages 1-45, by Alicia Forsberg, Eryn J. Adams and Nelson Cowan.
The abstract states that convincing correlational evidence suggests working memory ability is related to various measures of educational attainment.
The authors consider the working memory system as a bottleneck for long-term learning, constraining the ability to learn the meaning of new concepts and encode new information.
The abstract says prior knowledge allows people to categorize and chunk information.
The abstract describes a positive feedback loop in which better working memory allows more knowledge accumulation, which helps offload working memory to long-term memory.

The introduction states that working memory capacity is highly limited, while people seem able to retain essentially unlimited information in long-term memory (citing Brady, Konkle, Alvarez, & Oliva, 2008).
The introduction notes that working memory capacity gradually increases as children grow older.

The introduction cites Gathercole, Pickering, Knight, & Stegmann (2004) for a large body of correlational research showing working memory capacity within an age group reliably predicts educational attainment.
The authors suggest adjusting learning materials according to learners' working memory abilities and long-term memory knowledge may allow the most efficient learning.
The implications section states that poorer working memory predicts lower attainment in mathematics, reading, and science in school-aged children.

The chapter's sections cover long-term learning, working memory, the relationship between working and long-term memory, working memory limits in long-term learning, long-term memory's role in working memory, and practical application.
The chapter has 229 references and is cited by 7 works according to the page.
